usage: destination 에: 교실에 가다 = go to the classroom
우리 here means 'my/our' group's room, very natural
examples: Simple location question; 이 marks the subject of 어디예요
I chat with a friend in the classroom.
에서 = the place an action happens; 하고 = 'with'
Class ended, so the students left the classroom.
나가다 takes 에서 (out from a place), never 에
nuance: 교실 is Sino-Korean 教室 — 教 'teach' + 室 'room', literally 'teaching room', i.e. the single physical room where one class meets. The key contrast is 교실 vs 학교(學校 'school'): 학교 is the whole institution/campus, while 교실 is just one room inside it — so 'I'm at school' is 학교에 있어요, not 교실에 있어요 unless you literally mean the room. Also distinguish 교실 (the room) from 수업(授業, the lesson/class period that takes place in it). The everyday particle split is the trap for English speakers: use 에 when the room is a destination you move toward (교실에 들어가다 'enter the classroom'), but 에서 when you do an activity inside it (교실에서 발표하다 'present in the classroom'). English 'in the classroom' maps to 에서 only for actions; for static existence you say 교실에 있다.

structuredNuance.t: 교실 is the single physical room where one class meets.

usage: The fixed verb is 하다, never 만들다; object takes 를
많다 = many/much; the amount is the subject, so 가
내다 = submit/turn in (also 제출하다, more formal)
Noun-noun compound; 숙제 takes the subject as a modifier
examples: Did you finish all your homework?
Casual question; 다 = 'all/completely', a very common collocation with 하다
별로 + negative = 'not really/not much'; amount is the subject (가)
I forgot the homework and didn't bring it.
깜빡하다 = 'absent-mindedly forget', the natural verb students use
nuance: 숙제 is Sino-Korean 宿題 — 宿 'lodging/stay overnight' + 題 'topic/problem', literally a 'problem to take home overnight', i.e. work a teacher assigns to be done outside class. The verb is locked: Koreans say 숙제를 하다 'do homework', and 숙제를 내다 means a student turns it in (while a teacher 내다 a 숙제 means 'assign/set' it — context decides). Contrast 숙제 with 공부(工夫, 'study') and 과제(課題, 'assignment/coursework'): 공부하다 is the broad act of studying anything, whereas 숙제 is a specific assigned task, and 과제 is the more formal university word for a project or paper. The big English-speaker pitfall is translating 'do my homework' as 숙제를 만들다 'make homework' (✗ — that sounds like you created the assignment) or 숙제를 공부하다 (✗); the only natural pairing is 숙제를 하다.

usage: Fixed verb is 보다 (literally 'see'), never 하다
Existence/scheduling; the exam is the subject, so 이
붙다 'stick' = pass, 떨어지다 'fall' = fail; both take 에
기말(期末) = end of term; cf. 중간 시험 = midterm
examples: Casual; 있어요 used for a scheduled event existing
I took the Korean exam yesterday.
봤어요 = past of 보다; the set phrase 시험을 보다
I studied hard so I passed the exam.
Pass = 시험에 붙다; note the particle is 에, not 를
nuance: 시험 is Sino-Korean 試驗 — 試 'try/test' + 驗 'examine', literally 'a trial examination'. The collocation English speakers must memorize is 시험을 보다 — Koreans 'see' an exam, they do not 'do' it, so 시험을 하다 is wrong. Passing and failing are vivid metaphors with the particle 에: 시험에 붙다 (literally 'stick to the exam') = pass, 시험에 떨어지다 ('fall off the exam') = fail — note these take 에, not 을. Contrast 시험 with 퀴즈(quiz, a small in-class test) and with 검사(檢査, an inspection/medical test like 건강 검사): a graded school test is always 시험, never 퀴즈 unless it is a tiny informal one. The classic 직역 trap is 'take an exam' → 시험을 가지다/취하다 ✗ (English 'take' never transfers); and learners often write 시험을 통과하다, which is understandable but bookish — the everyday word is 붙다.

usage: 듣다 'listen' is the set verb for attending a class
Scheduling; the class is the subject, so 이
늦다 takes 에 for the event you're late to
Subject-noun modifier; cf. 수학 수업 'math class'
examples: Casual schedule check; 있어요 for a class existing on the timetable
수업을 듣다 = attend; 열심히 = 'diligently', a habitual collocation
I'm sorry for being late to class.
늦다 + 에 marks the event; -아서 gives the reason
nuance: 수업 is Sino-Korean 授業 — 授 'give/confer' + 業 'work/study', literally 'conferring instruction', i.e. the lesson or class session itself (the activity and time period). The set verb is 수업을 듣다 'listen to a class' = attend/take it; from the teacher's side it is 수업을 하다 'give/teach a class'. Three near-neighbors confuse learners: 수업 (the lesson event) vs 교실(教室, the room it happens in) vs 과목(科目, the subject like 'math' or 'history') vs 강의(講義, a university lecture). So 'I have three classes today' = 수업 세 개, but 'I take three subjects' = 과목 세 개. The English-speaker pitfall is using 하다 to mean 'take a class' (수업을 하다 actually means 'to teach', which is what a professor does) — as a student you 듣다 a class. Also, 'go to class' is 수업에 가다 (event as destination with 에).

usage: Object takes 를; everyday shopping verb 사다
Counter is 권 (for bound paper goods), not 개
새 is a pre-noun modifier; no 의 needed
examples: I organize vocabulary in my notebook.

Please give me just one notebook.
권 counts bound books; 만 = 'just/only'; 주세요 = polite request
nuance: 공책 is Sino-Korean 空冊 — 空 'empty' + 冊 'book/volume', literally an 'empty book', i.e. a blank bound notebook for writing in. Because it is a 冊, it is counted with the unit 권 (공책 한 권), exactly like 책 'book' — counting it with 개 is the classic foreigner slip. In real life Koreans very often just say the English loanword 노트 (from 'note'); 공책 sounds slightly more textbook/childlike, while 노트 is the casual everyday choice, and a 'notebook computer' is 노트북 — don't confuse the three. Contrast 공책 (paper to write in) with 교과서(教科書, 'textbook' you read from) and 수첩(手帖, a small pocket planner/memo book). The English-speaker pitfall is the counter (use 권, not 개) and assuming 'notebook' must be 공책 — in conversation 노트 is more natural, and never let 노트북 slip in when you mean the paper kind.

usage: 깎다 = shave/sharpen, the set verb for pencils
Counter 자루 for long thin sticks (pens, brushes)
examples: 좀 softens the request; 빌려주다 = lend (to me)
저는 시험 볼 때 연필로 써요.
I write with a pencil when taking exams.
The pencil is blunt, so I need to sharpen it.
nuance: 연필 is Sino-Korean 鉛筆 — 鉛 'lead' + 筆 'writing brush/pen', literally 'lead pen', the wooden graphite pencil. The instrument particle 로/으로 is essential: you write 연필로 ('with/by means of a pencil'), and the matching verb for upkeep is 연필을 깎다 'shave the pencil' = sharpen it. The counter 자루 is used for long slender objects (pens, pencils, brushes, even umbrellas) — 연필 한 자루 — so don't default to 개. Contrast the writing tools clearly: 연필 (pencil, erasable) vs 볼펜(ballpoint pen) vs 샤프(mechanical 'sharp' pencil) vs 펜(pen, general). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle — 'write with a pencil' must be 연필로, not 연필을 (학생이 연필을 써요 means 'uses a pencil' as an object, fine, but 'by means of' is 연필로); and English 'sharpen' tempts learners toward a 'make sharp' calque, when the idiomatic verb is the everyday 깎다 (the same verb used for peeling fruit).

usage: Tool particle 로 + the verb 지우다 it derives from
빌리다 = borrow (from someone); object takes 를
Small everyday item often counted with native 하나/한 개
examples: I write with a pencil and erase with an eraser.
Parallel 로 ... 로 for two tools; 지우개로 지우다
Could you lend me an eraser?
-ㄹ 수 있다 = 'can'; a polite, softer request than 주세요
nuance: 지우개 is a pure native-Korean word (not Sino-Korean): the verb stem 지우- 'to erase/remove' + the productive suffix -개 'a tool/instrument for ~ing'. That -개 pattern is worth learning because it builds many tool nouns the same way — 베다→베개 'pillow (cutting-rest tool)', 덮다→덮개 'cover', 따다→따개 'opener' — so 지우개 transparently means 'erasing-tool'. It pairs naturally with 연필 (you erase pencil, 연필로 쓴 것을 지우개로 지우다) and the tool particle is 로: 지우개로 지우다. Watch the verb/noun split: 지우다 is the verb 'to erase' and 지우개 is the object; a beginner who says 지우개해요 for 'I erase' is mixing them — the verb is 지워요. Korean erasers are often called 고무지우개 ('rubber eraser') when emphasizing material, and a whiteboard eraser is 칠판지우개.

usage: Position noun 앞; 칠판 앞에 서다 'stand in front of the board'
examples: The teacher wrote the answer on the board.
에 marks the writing surface; 썼어요 past of 쓰다
I couldn't see the board, so I moved forward.
보이다 'be visible' (≠ 보다); -아서 gives the reason
nuance: 칠판 is Sino-Korean 漆板 — 漆 'lacquer/black paint' + 板 'board/plank', literally a 'lacquered (black) board', the writing board at the front of a classroom. The two everyday actions split by particle: write ON it = 칠판에 쓰다 (surface destination with 에), but look AT it = 칠판을 보다 (object with 를). Many modern rooms have a white 화이트보드 (whiteboard, written with markers) instead of a chalk 칠판, but 칠판 still serves as the generic word for 'the board'. A subtle contrast English speakers miss: 보다 'look at' the board is intentional looking, whereas 보이다 'the board is/ isn't visible' is the spontaneous can-see verb — '칠판이 안 보여요' = 'I can't see the board', not '칠판을 안 봐요' ('I'm not looking at the board'). The pitfall is keeping the particles straight: 에 for writing on, 을 for looking at, and reaching for 보이다 (not 보다) when the issue is visibility.

usage: Time point/period takes 에: 방학에 여행하다
School 'goes on vacation'; 하다 here = the break begins
Season + 방학; cf. 겨울 방학 'winter break'
끝나다 = come to an end; subject takes 이
examples: I want to go to Korea during the break.
에 marks the time; -고 싶다 = 'want to'
I worked a part-time job during the break.
동안 = 'for the duration of'; a very common time collocation
nuance: 방학 is Sino-Korean 放學 — 放 'release/let go' + 學 'studies', literally 'releasing (from) studies', i.e. the official school break between terms (summer/winter). The crucial contrast is 방학 vs 휴가(休暇, 'leave/holiday'): 방학 belongs to the school calendar and applies to students/teachers, while 휴가 is the time off a worker takes from a job — a salaried adult on vacation is 휴가 중, never 방학 중. Also distinguish 방학 (a scheduled school break) from 휴일(休日, a single day off / public holiday like a national holiday) and 연휴(連休, a string of consecutive holidays). Note 방학을 하다 means '(the school) goes on break / break starts', an event, not 'I take a vacation'. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a working adult's trip 방학 (it must be 휴가), and forgetting that 'during vacation' uses the time particle 에 (방학에) or the duration noun 동안 (방학 동안), not 에서.

Saying 방학에서 for 'during vacation' ✗. A time period takes 에 (방학에) or 동안 (방학 동안); 에서 is for places/actions.
Confusing 방학 (a multi-week term break) with 휴일 (a single day off) or 연휴 (a holiday stretch).

usage: Set verb is 하다; 질문하다 is one word too
Existence; the question is the subject, so 이
답하다 takes 에 for the question being answered
받다 = receive; what a speaker does at Q&A
examples: I asked the teacher a question.
께 = honorific 'to' (for a teacher); 질문을 하다 = ask
Good question. Let's think about it together.
좋은 질문 is a fixed compliment; -아 보다 = 'try ~ing'
nuance: 질문 is Sino-Korean 質問 — 質 'substance/inquire into' + 問 'ask', literally 'to inquire and ask', i.e. a question put to someone. The set verb is 질문을 하다 (or the single verb 질문하다); the person you ask takes 에게/한테 (or honorific 께 for a teacher): 선생님께 질문을 하다. Its natural partner is 대답/답(答) — a 질문 is answered by a 대답. The big redundancy trap for English speakers is 질문을 물어보다 ✗: 물어보다 already means 'to ask', so this literally says 'ask a question-asking' — say either 질문을 하다 or just 물어보다, never both. Distinguish 질문 (a question seeking information/an answer) from 문제(問題, a 'problem' or exam item) — '3 questions on the test' are 문제 세 개, but 'I have a question for you' is 질문이 있어요. Note answering takes 에: 질문에 답하다, not 질문을 답하다.

Using 를 to answer: 질문을 답하다 ✗. 답하다 takes 에: 질문에 답하다 / 질문에 대답하다.
Using 질문 for an exam item. A test question/problem is 문제; 질문 is a question you ask a person for an answer.

usage: Set verb 하다; 대답하다 is the one-word form
The thing answered takes 에, not 를
듣다 = hear; what the asker does
examples: 대답이 없다 = no reply; 이 marks the subject
큰 소리로 = 'in a loud voice'; 대답하다 as one verb
질문에 (에, not 를) + 대답하다; -아 주세요 = polite request
nuance: 대답 is Sino-Korean 對答 — 對 'face/respond-to' + 答 'reply', literally 'a facing reply', i.e. the spoken/written response to a question or call. It is the natural partner of 질문(質問): a 질문 is met by a 대답, and the verb is 대답을 하다 / 대답하다. The sharp contrast to master is 대답 vs 정답(正答, 正 'correct' + 答): 대답 is simply 'a/the response someone gives' (it can be right or wrong), while 정답 is specifically 'the correct answer' to a problem — so on a quiz '정답은 3번이에요' = 'the correct answer is number 3', but 그 학생의 대답 = 'that student's response'. Also note 답 alone is a shorter everyday form of both. The particle pitfall mirrors 질문: you answer a question with 에 — 질문에 대답하다 / 질문에 답하다, NOT 질문을 대답하다. English 'answer the phone/door' does not use 대답 either — that is 전화를 받다 / 문을 열다.

usage: look something up in a dictionary
Set verb 찾다 'search/find'; object takes 를
Source/location of the search takes 에서
Language + 사전; cf. 영어 사전 'English dictionary'
찾아보다 adds the 'try/check' nuance to 찾다
examples: I look up unknown words in the dictionary.
에서 marks where you search; 사전에서 찾다
요즘은 종이 사전보다 앱을 더 많이 써요.
These days I use an app more than a paper dictionary.

The notorious pitfall for learners is the near-homophone pair 사전(辭典, dictionary) vs 사진(寫眞, photograph) — one letter apart (ㅓ vs ㅣ) but completely different; mixing them up ('I took a 사전' for a photo) is a classic slip. Also distinguish 사전 from 백과사전(百科事典, encyclopedia — note the different middle hanja 事 'matters') and from 단어장 (a personal vocabulary list/flashcards). Today most learners use a phone 사전 app rather than a 종이 사전 'paper dictionary'. English 'look up' transfers fine to 찾다, but remember to use 에서 for the dictionary as the place searched, while the word you seek takes 를.
